title: Luonnontieteellisen museon Elämän historia -sali sulkeutuu tammikuussa – uusi näyttely avautuu loppuvuodesta 2028
content:
The Natural History Museum’s History of Life is one of the museum’s most popular exhibitions. However, the exhibition, completed in 2008, has long been in need of an update, as it is outdated both in terms of content and exhibition technology.

– The new exhibition will present evolution and the development of biodiversity in a more spectacular and tangible way than before. This is the museum’s most significant renewal project in years, says Sanna Vuori, Head of the Public Engagement Unit at the Finnish Museum of Natural History.

The dinosaurs Giganotosaurus carolinii and Shunosaurus lii in the History of Life exhibition have become familiar to many museum visitors over the years. They will remain in the new exhibition but will be joined by never-before-seen reconstructions of prehistoric animals. Among other things, a reconstruction of the otter-like early whale Ambulocetus natans is currently being built in the museum’s conservation facilities.

title: Southnord Artfest 2026: Roots en Route
content:
Plants have always travelled – with the wind, with animals and birds, with humans. They have been carried across oceans, taken from their habitats and replanted to serve trade and empire.

Roots en Route is a multi-sensory installation by four artists who will create a multi-sensory installation in dialogue with the greenhouses – examining rootedness and displacement; asking what grows where it was planted and what survives the crossing. The African plants that fill the greenhouses carry their own histories of movement and adaptation.

Camille Norment in collaboration with Sofia Jernberg create a soundscape drawing on the insects and birds of the plants' homelands. Toubab Holmes' site-specific scent installation traces the hidden journeys of plants through the extractive system of perfumery. Charmaine Watkiss visits the botanical legacies and healing traditions of her Caribbean ancestry through large-scale drawings of Plant Warriors. Together, the three works read the botanical garden as an archive of movement, and the plants in it as things that were carried, taken and made to travel.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.

title: Africa and Europe join forces for One Health at Think Corner in World One Health Day event
content:
The event "Africa-Europe Collaboration in One Health" takes place on Wednesday 4 November 2026 at 17:00–19:00 at Think Corner (Tiedekulma) in Helsinki. It is organised by and , and it is open to everyone. The event can also be followed .

The programme opens with short talks from researchers. Professor Tarja Sironen, who also chairs the event, will speak about outbreak response. Senior University Lecturer Leena Hanski will explore how local knowledge and biodiversity can support health management in West Africa. Professor Johanna Lindahl will discuss how the Sustainable Development Goals can work together instead of against each other.

Professor Enrico Di Minin will present the Taita Research Station in Kenya as a hub for One Health partnerships. University Researcher Johanna Muurinen, chair of One Health Finland, will share insights from fieldwork on waste management and antimicrobial resistance. Professor Frederick Stoddard will talk about crop diversity, healthy diets and research done together with farmers.

title: Kunnostustyöt tehostavat Pääjärven vesiensuojelua
content:

Koiransuolenoja, which flows into Lake Pääjärvi, has long been a site for water quality monitoring by Lammi Biological Station. In 2013, sedimentation basins were constructed in the stream to reduce the load of suspended solids and nutrients entering the lake. While these basins have been effective at retaining suspended solids, there is a desire to further improve their performance—specifically to enhance nutrient retention. 

The ongoing restoration involves replacing one of the bottom weirs within the last sedimentation basin. The weisis being constructed using a nature-based design that allows for the free movement of fish within the stream. The restoration is being carried out in close cooperation with local landowners, facilitating long-term water protection efforts and research.

Eligibility: All Urbaria members, and future members with pending membership applications are welcome to apply. Collaboration between different universities and research institutes is encouraged, but the main applicant has to be affiliated with the University of Helsinki.

title: Seminar on The History of Small Towns and Cities: Finland and the World
content:
Date: 19 November 2026
Time: 15.00-17.00
Place: B214 (Hall 4), Metsätalo (Unioninkatu 40, Helsinki)
 
Programme:
 
Opening Remarks
Laura Kolbe, Emerita Professor of European History, University of Helsinki
 
Nuclei for an Urban Nation - Small towns in Finland from 1810s to the present
Matti O. Hannikainen, Docent, University of Helsinki

Abstract: 
The last two centuries witnessed the gradual transition of Finland from an agrarian to an urban society. The advent of new industries coupled with new modes of transportation provided the momentum for economic growth for numerous smaller towns after the 1850s. The urbanization thus continued the tradition of a top-down urban policy and process to boost commerce, while new urbanizing communities grew up as local hubs for trade, industries, and transportation with local impetus from below. Yet most of the 37 Finnish towns in 1900 were small. Thew new century witnessed a profound societal change due to continuous population growth, however. While Finnish society urbanized, national policies did not support the process wholeheartedly. Until the 1960s, the aim of Finnish policies was to control urbanization, which partially explains the small size of many Finnish towns and townships. With accelerated urban growth after the Second World War, the creation of new towns after 1960 was seen as a way of regaining political control over the urbanization process and invigorating trade and industrial development across the country with limited success in longer perspective. Hence, at the advent of the 21st century, Finnish small towns remain a heterogenous group and their position is under pressure again.

Why Study Small Towns? Their Importance in Global Perspective
Peter Clark, Emeritus Professor of European Urban History, University of Helsinki

Abstract: Too often neglected in the urban literature and public debate, small towns (from the Middle Ages to now) have housed a significant part of the urban population and played a key role in urban development, at the regional, national and global level. The recently published book by Emeritus Professor Peter Clark, Small Towns and Cities in World History (2026), sheds new and important light on their trajectory and multi-functionality up to the present day.

title: Making medieval history add up
content:
Rows, columns, colour-coded cells and endless filters are hardly the stuff of historical adventure. But for us in the CHARM project, spreadsheets are becoming an important tool for asking new questions about medieval books and documents.

Our research brings together several types of information. Through species identification, we can investigate which animals provided the skins used to make parchment. The Parchment Quality Index (PQI) helps us assess differences in parchment quality. Historical information, such as the dates and origins of documents, provides another layer of evidence, connecting these material characteristics to the people and places behind medieval written culture.

Individually, each dataset tells us something different. Together, they open up new possibilities. Do documents produced around the same time share material characteristics? Does parchment quality vary between different groups of documents? Can we identify patterns that might help us understand how writing practices developed in medieval Finland?

title: Vieroitusoireisten vastasyntyneiden hoitoa kehitetään Jorvin sairaalan ja Helsingin yliopiston yhteistutkimuksessa
content:
Helsingin Sanomien 20.10.2026 julkaistussa artikkelissa kerrottiin, miten huumausaineille raskausaikana altistuneita vastasyntyneitä hoidetaan Jorvin sairaalassa. Artikkelissa kerrottiin muun muassa osastolla vierailevista vapaaehtoisista, joiden tärkeänä tehtävänä on tarjota vauvoille syliä, hoivaa ja lohtua. Samassa yhteydessä mainittiin myös Jorvissa käynnissä olevasta tutkimuksesta vieroitusoireisten vastasyntyneiden parissa.

Kyseessä on HUS:n ja Helsingin yliopiston yhteinen tutkimus, jossa selvitetään vieroitusoireiden patofysiologiaa ja kehitetään uusia lääkkeettömiä hoitomuotoja vauvojen hyvinvoinnin tukemiseksi. Helsingin yliopiston tutkijatohtori ja vastasyntyneiden teho-osaston musiikkiterapeutti Kaisamari Kostilainen on kehittänyt moniaistillisen intervention, jonka tarkoituksena on rauhoittaa vieroitusoireisen vauvan olotilaa eri aistikanavien kautta (syli, liike, katsekontakti, hyräily/laulu).
